utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-R77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson. Ms. Marosevic, you remain subject to your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marosevic, I have a few more questions I would like to put to you today. When we stopped yesterday, we had been talking about a trip that you made to Tuzla to speak to the mother of Mirsad Sahanic and get his phone number. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you made that trip to Tuzla? Do you recall what month that was?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It was sometime last year in 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I think so, yes. At the end of '98.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: At the end of '98, you mean like November or December?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you are the one that gave the phone number to Mr. Agnes, so that Mr. Agnes could call Mirsad. So obviously this trip to Tuzla took place before Mr. Agnes called Mirsad?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did this trip take place before you introduced Mr. Agnes to Mr. Avramovic, or to Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Before. Before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, this trip to Tuzla took place before Mr. Agnes had even told you, according to your version, that he was willing to testify for Milan Simic, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So before you had even discussed the possibility with Mr. Agnes of his testifying for Milan Simic, and also discuss that maybe he should call his friend Mirsad, you had already gotten in your mind that you should get in touch with Mirsad and get his phone number, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. Agnes who suggested you get in touch with Mirsad; it was someone else, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I did myself at my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, the reason that you had to go to Tuzla to get this phone number from Mirsad's mother is that, obviously, Mr. Simic couldn't travel to Tuzla, could he?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It probably would also be awkward for Mr. Avramovic to travel to Tuzla as well, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, we didn't talk. There was no need for him to go. I asked for the number for my own benefit, not because of Mr. Simic or Mr. Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So your getting in touch with Mirsad had absolutely nothing to do with trying to get Mirsad to agree to testify for Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just a total coincidence that this came up, after you had discussed it with Mr. Agnes, and Mr. Agnes pointed out that perhaps Mirsad could be a witness as well? Just a coincidence all this happens; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, when Mirsad Sahanic testified here, he told the Court that during one of your phone conversations, that you had mentioned to him, if he couldn't meet you in Bosnia, that you were going to be travelling on a business trip to the Netherlands, and perhaps you could meet at the German border. Could you tell the Court what business it is that you had in the Netherlands that would cause you to travel to this country?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I have some relatives here, and I was going to go and stay with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Didn't have anything to do with the fact that the Tribunal is located in the Netherlands? Again, just an interesting coincidence?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, let's move on, then, to another subject. Also during your phone conversations with Mirsad, Mirsad told you that, understandably, having been detained in prison camps, he was reluctant to return to Bosanski Samac. He was concerned about his safety. Do you recall discussing that with him on the phone?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you told him, according to Mirsad, that he shouldn't worry -- this is Mirsad's words -- because you were in charge, and you could guarantee his safety if he went to Bosanski Samac. Do you recall telling him that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Everybody was going to Bosanski Samac, without any problems. So there was no need for anybody to be afraid of coming to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Everybody was going to Bosanski Samac, the witnesses who are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said everybody was going to Bosanski Samac. I can list at least 50 or 60 people I know who were prepared to come and testify here, who are not going to Bosanski Samac because they are concerned about their safety.

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, some people are even going back home to Bosanski Samac. I don't know why they would be concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But Mirsad did express to you his own concerns about his safety in not wanting to return to Bosanski Samac, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: How do you mean that he did not want to go back?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, didn't Mirsad say something to you to the effect that he had reservations about going to Bosanski Samac because he didn't know if he would feel safe?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And he didn't think he would feel safe because during the war he had been arrested and detained and beaten and otherwise mistreated, for several months, so of course he didn't want to return to that town, did he?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But you told him that there was no reason to be afraid, and that you could guarantee there was no reason that he should be afraid; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't any reason. I didn't say that I could guarantee anything. I just said that there was no reason for him to be afraid of going to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Marosevic, you also said that you saw Mr. Agnes in Bosanski Samac in May of 1993, when he was in the army of the Republika Srpska. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, in your conversations with Mr. Agnes, did he tell you that he had been involved in an accidental shooting, where a young woman was shot when his gun discharged? Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I heard that afterwards, but not from Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Agnes did tell the Court about that, and he explained that that happened a few weeks after he joined the VRS, which was in late December, 1992. So in May of 1993, Mr. Agnes was in gaol in Pelagicevo, on charges of shooting this young girl. So how could you have seen him in Bosanski Samac in May, if he was in gaol in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Because I know that my boss opened the cafe in March, 1993, and two months later Mr. Agnes came.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But, according to Mr. Agnes, and essentially according as well to Mr. Haynes and the questions he put to him, he was in gaol for most of 1993 and didn't get out until October. So is it possible your recollection of the dates is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. If he was in prison, he was in a detention centre, pre-trial, and you stay there for 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also said that at no time, so far as you know, did Mr. Agnes ever meet Milan Simic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, he never met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But you testified earlier that it was when you were having a conversation with Mr. Agnes, during the course of the conversation you mentioned to him Milan Simic and the fact that he was charged with having committed crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And during that conversation, Mr. Agnes, out of the blue, volunteered that he would be willing to testify for Milan Simic, didn't he? According to you.

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: When we spoke, he said that he knew Mr. Simic from sight, by sight, and that Mr. Simic had done nothing wrong, and that he would help, and he would tell anybody to help him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you then at some point in time told Mr. Simic, "By the way, Milan, I've got a man who is willing to come and testify for you; isn't that great?" You probably had a conversation along those lines, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, I asked Mr. Simic for the telephone number of his lawyer, Drago Vukovic, and he gave me his phone number, so that Mr. Simic had no contact at all with Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But that's not my question. You told Milan Simic that Mr. Agnes was willing to testify on his behalf, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I don't actually remember the conversation we had, exactly. Perhaps. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Don't you think it's something you might have mentioned to Milan Simic, that you had come across a person that was willing to come to The Hague and testify for him?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember. Maybe I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, let's assume, then, for the sake of argument, that at some point in time you told Milan Simic that Mr. Agnes was willing to testify for him. Wouldn't it be logical that Mr. Simic would be quite grateful to Mr. Agnes and might want to meet him and shake his hand and say "Thank you very much, Mr. Agnes, for agreeing to testify for me"? You're saying that nothing like that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, nothing like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that -- going back to this first meeting that you just mentioned between Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Agnes, you said that you actually introduced them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And this was at the cafe where you were working?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, it was in the Jetset Cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And was there some reason why this meeting took place at the Jetset instead of the Cafe Lotos, as all the other meetings had?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, it was just by chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And are you familiar with a company call Nova Forma? Have you ever heard of a company by that name?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It's a business that exists in Bosanski Samac; right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did Milan Simic ever have any business interests in that company?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So as far as you know, it is possible that he might have had some business interests in that company?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you obviously didn't spend every minute of every day with Mr. Milan Simic, did you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So it's not impossible that at some point in time, unbeknownst to you, Mr. Agnes might in fact have had a meeting with Milan Simic, and you just didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about it. But I do believe that Agnes would have told me, had he had a meeting with Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, I asked you when you started your testimony yesterday if you had ever discussed the case with Mr. Avramovic, and I believe that you said you had not discussed the case with Mr. Avramovic. What is the correct answer to that? Have you discussed the case in any detail with Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: With Mr. Avramovic, I only spoke to him when he came to ask me to tell him everything I knew about Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So he did talk to you, then, about Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And he told you what Mr. Agnes had said to him?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, how could you have a discussion about Mr. Agnes, then, if he didn't tell you anything about Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic came to me and asked me whether I would be willing to say everything I knew about Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Ms. Marosevic, I just want to clarify something. Yesterday, and I'm referring to page 556 of the transcript, line 22; I'm going to read a question and an answer to you, Ms. Marosevic. Question -- this was put to you by

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Did you have a discussion with Mr. Avramovic about what Mr. Agnes had told him?" Your answer: "He told me, Mr. Avramovic told me that he had spoken to Mr. Agnes and that he would get in touch with him. I know he referred to an event, that Mr. Agnes had told him that he had been travelling through Samac. I found that strange because I knew that he had stayed at the hotel. And I said that that was not true." Do you recall that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think this question ought to be clarified, because of course that question relates to 1998. The question that Ms. Paterson began with was a question asking this witness whether she has ever discussed this case with Mr. Avramovic. So I think the witness may be confused, and I think Ms. Paterson ought to clarify what it is she is asking about, whether she is asking about the Bosanski Samac case in general or the Rule 77 proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Marosevic, let me ask you: Did you understand my question, or do you not understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would like to know, too, I'm afraid, Ms. Paterson. Could we have an answer? Which one are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Avramovic ever tell you any of the facts that Mr. Agnes told him about what happened in Bosanski Samac during the war, and particularly involving Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Avramovic ever tell you anything about conversations he had with Mr. Agnes about any subject?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned that Mr. Agnes had told him that he was passing through Samac on the way to Vienna. This was strange to me, because we all know in Samac that Mr. Agnes lived in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is that Mr. Avramovic, on at least one occasion, discussed with you details of what Mr. Agnes had told him; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, that's all he told me, what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Marosevic, I'd like to go to the famous blue bag that we've seen on several occasions here that Mr. Agnes admitted was his bag and which you claim was left at your house when he left to come and get in touch with the Tribunal. Do you know the bag I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that you found that bag in your house in May of 1999; is that right? Or sometime after Mr. Agnes --

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you did not turn the bag over to Mr. Avramovic until September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So for five months, that bag sat in your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And the bag was not locked, was it? It didn't have a lock on it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You didn't put it in a cabinet and lock the door, did you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I put it in the cupboard, but I didn't lock the cupboard door.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And obviously you're not the only person that lives in your house and enters your house, are you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your father lives there, your brother lives there, and I imagine from time to time you have friends and company that comes to visit, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So it's entirely possible that any time during those five months, any one of those people could have come and opened that bag and taken things out, and put things in, and taken them out, and put things in, so there's really no way we have of knowing, other than your word for it, what was in that bag when you found it in May, do we?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, but my friends don't go looking into my cupboard for them to be able to put something in there, friends that come to visit me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But you put something in that bag, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, his towels.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. So everything that was in that bag was not exactly as it was when you found it, was it? You added something: You added the towels.

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, Agnes's towels, because everything was jumbled up in the bag.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: For all we know, you added the ID card, and the letter from the ICRC, and any of the other items in there, you could have added or anyone else could have added during that time; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: But where would I get his army booklet from, or anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, there's a good question, Ms. Marosevic. I was going to ask you that question myself. You said earlier that you agreed that a large number of Croats, and for that matter Muslims, had left Bosanski Samac during the war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, but many people stayed, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, but many left, and many were quite desperate to get out of town, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you wouldn't be surprised to learn that a lot of those people used false identification and false IDs to get out on occasion; they had to go and get false IDs to get out of town? You probably know some people that did that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It probably wouldn't come as a surprise to you that it's not hard at all on the black market in Bosnia and Bosanski Samac to obtain false identifications; that doesn't come as a surprise to you, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We are entering into the realms of fiction and moving away from the realms of the evidence in this case. She says she doesn't know people like that. I don't think that entitles Ms. Paterson to make a speech on her knowledge of general practice in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Paterson; I think you are going a little too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why don't you put it to her expressly that she put that document in the bag? That's what you're really after, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, that and some other things, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But Ms. Marosevic, in answer to the Judge's question, did you put that identification card in the bag?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. The army booklet was in the bag.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did anyone ever come and ask you to get false identification for them? Mr. Agnes or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: At any time, did anyone -- Mr. Agnes, any of your other friends or acquaintances -- ever come to you and ask you to help them get false identification?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, did you tell Mirsad Sahanic something to that effect in one of your phone conversations, that Mr. Agnes had asked you to get him some false ID?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. Mr. Agnes asked me for an ID card, how he could get an ID card in Bosanski Samac, and I told him that he had to register and then get the document in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think Mr. Sahanic told a somewhat different version of that, but I'll leave that to the Judges to compare the two versions of that conversation. Now, Mr. Agnes, before he left your house, and again I am accepting, just for the sake of argument, your version of the facts, that Mr. Agnes was staying at your house and left the blue bag there. I don't concede that. We'll just say that for sake of argument. He never told you that he was planning to leave and come to get in touch with the Tribunal, did he?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, he never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And that probably came as a big surprise to you, when you found out that he had contacted the Tribunal; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You weren't at all surprised when you found out that Mr. Agnes had contacted the Tribunal and told the Tribunal that Mr. Avramovic and Mr. Simic were trying to force him to testify for Mr. Simic? That didn't surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's about four questions. Could it be broken down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did it surprise you that Mr. Agnes came to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think about it really much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did it surprise you to learn that Mr. Agnes told the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You better establish that she did learn that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marosevic, do you know why we are here today, the purpose of this hearing?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I am hearing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: No. Do you know why you are here to testify before the Court?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: All I know is that I have to say everything I know about Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did anyone ever tell you that Mr. Avramovic is charged with forcing, attempting to force Mr. Agnes to testify on behalf of Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, do you know that or not? Did you know that before you came to Court today, Ms. Marosevic? Did you know what Mr. Avramovic was charged with?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Milan Simic is charged with trying to pressure Mr. Agnes into testifying before this Court in favour of Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You didn't know that before you came to Court yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: When did you first find that out, that Mr. Agnes had accused Milan Simic of trying to force him to testify before this Court?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: When I came here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So why was it, then, that you took the blue bag to Mr. Avramovic that Mr. Agnes left behind? What interest could it have been to Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, when we spoke, I mentioned the fact of the bag being at my place, and Mr. Avramovic asked me about the bag, and I said, "Well, if you need it, here you are. Here is the bag." That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Paterson, the witness has just told us that she learnt that there was pressure on the part of Milan Simic on Witness Agnes, for him to testify in his favour. The witness has just told us that she learned that upon arriving in The Hague, that is, before appearing in Court, before appearing in this Trial Chamber. I should like you to ask the witness from whom she learnt that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marosevic, did you understand the Judge's question? He would like to know who told you about these charges against Milan Simic. How did you learn of that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't remember. In one of the conversations, when we were sitting together, somebody mentioned it. I don't remember exactly who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You don't remember if it was Mr. Avramovic that told you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You don't remember if it was Milan Simic that told you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I didn't see Mr. Simic until I came here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Ms. Paterson, Ms. Marosevic could tell us whom she saw when she arrived at The Hague, because she said it was during a conversation. Who was she talking to when she arrived in The Hague and before she appeared in Court?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: With Mr. Peter. I spoke to Mr. Peter. He asked me questions, and I provided answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Peter?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So by "Mr. Peter," you mean Mr. Haynes, the attorney for Mr. Avramovic and Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that Mr. Haynes told you that there were charges against Mr. Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly who it was, but somebody said it. I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Marosevic, that military ID card that you referred to that you claim you found in that blue bag, are you aware of the fact -- did you take any time to read that closely?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Not very closely, but I did look through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And can we have the ID card, have it shown to the witness, please. Okay. You have that ID card in front of you, Ms. Marosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So when you, as you claim, took it out of the blue bag, did you read through the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On which occasion are you putting?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Ever. Any time. The moment you took it out, any time since then, have you ever read through that entire document?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Not the whole document, but I did look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you looked at the first couple of pages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you can see from those first couple of pages that some things on that document have been changed, can't you? It's quite obvious to anyone that some things have been changed there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: It was in this condition when I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But, as you said, you didn't read through the entire document, so you have no way of knowing whether the information in that document is accurate and correct, do you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, but I read the first and second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But you didn't read the other 36 pages? You explained yesterday there were 38 pages to the document.

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But you are not in any position to know whether the information in there is correct or not, are you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the only question I have about that. Now, Ms. Marosevic, you said that you stayed in Bosanski Samac throughout the war years and right up until the present. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And during that time did you stay in your family apartment, the apartment that your family was living in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Is that the same apartment you are still living in today?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And except for that period of about seven days, when you said you were detained at the beginning of the war, did you live in that apartment since 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you are a Croat; correct, Ms. Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marosevic, are you aware that there was a decision issued on the 15th of May, 1992, by the municipal crisis staff of Bosanski Samac, in which it was ordered that all people of Croatian nationality on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac should be isolated and taken to vital facilities in the town and villages? Are you aware of that decision that was issued in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you weren't forced to move out of your apartment, were you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Only for those seven days while we were detained. And after that we returned to our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So all the other Croats, except for you, had to move out of their houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How can she possibly know that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that many people were forced, many Croats were forced to move out of their houses, were moved to villages such as Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had to, but everyone didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But a number of people did, didn't they, Ms. Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you and your family didn't, did they?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, we didn't. Nobody was forcing us to go. We didn't have to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And that's because you are good friends with many of the people who run the town of Bosanski Samac and who were running it back then; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't have been detained for seven days if that was the case. My uncle stayed as well, and some other people also stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that you first met Milan Simic when you were working in the municipality building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you were serving coffee there? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Can you explain what -- was there some sort of a small restaurant or cafe there, or how did this work that you served coffee in the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: There was a canteen, a kitchen in the municipality building, and that is where we were working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And how did you get that job? Did you know somebody that was working there, or how did you start working at that position?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: There were some people in Samac -- I can't remember the name now. I can't remember the name exactly -- and they were assigning people to various posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So you were assigned to work at that job?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to work somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And did you have a choice or did you have to work at that job?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, I asked to work there. I wanted to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You were not forced to work at that job, were you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But isn't it a fact, Ms. Marosevic, that many, if not most, of the Croats and Muslims that remained in Bosanski Samac had to do forced labour and had to do other types of work?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am going to ask that you direct that she doesn't answer that question. When we started these proceedings, Ms. Paterson undertook that the scope of the Prosecution evidence and cross-examination would be limited to matters relevant to the Rule 77 proceedings. Very little of what she's putting is substantiated by any evidence in this case, and it's simply a question of her making a series of political speeches and putting them to the witness. And all these matters affect the trial and indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, can you explain the relevance to these proceedings of that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that the reason why Ms. Marosevic is cooperating with Mr. Simic and Mr. Avramovic is that she's obviously close friends with them, has an association with them, and has received certain special privileges as a result of her relationship, one of which is that, unlike many of the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, she did not have to do forced labour projects. I can't change the facts. Those are the facts as happened in 1992, Your Honour. I am attempting, as best as possible, not to get into the facts. We are not getting into any charges alleged against these defendants. But that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid it's not. It's not a fact in these proceedings, and if all that is sought to be put to this witness is that she is a friend and well connected with defendants on the indictment, then all that has already been put. If the Prosecution wanted to seek to establish details about what happened to non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, they could have served us with drafted admissions in relation to this. I don't have the case papers in the trial and indictment. I don't know whether I can accept any of these assertions or not. And they are not relevant to whether Mr. Agnes has told us the truth about contact he had with lawyers and Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could perhaps frame the question in a different way. That might solve the problem. But if you want to discuss it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are entitled to seek to tie her in, if I may put it that way, with the people who ran Bosanski Samac. You are entitled to attempt to do that. And so far as you are putting that she was able to work in a cafe and everything, haven't you made your point? If we have to have this fact admitted, then it may be better if it was put a little bit more carefully than you've put it so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: If you would let me, Your Honour, I will just put two more questions to her, and I'll try and rephrase it in a way that should be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marosevic, you said that a number of Croats did move to the village of Zasavica, is that correct, during the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever have to go to Zasavica and work in the fields and collect the food that was being grown in the fields?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever have to go to Zasavica and kill the animals and prepare food for the army?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever have to sweep the streets of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No. I was working in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, the Chamber feels that you have exhausted this point. Move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Hunt will ask some questions before re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've told us that you were not friendly with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You told us that you were not friendly with the people who ran the town of Bosanski Samac, and you've also told us that you were able to take food very regularly into Mirsad when he was in detention. Who allowed you to do that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: The guard. Everyone could carry food. The policeman who was on guard at the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The policeman was the one who let you in with the food; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Not inside. They would come out to the steps. We would see each other for a while, and we would give them food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you see other people doing that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but I saw some other women from Samac carrying food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I want to take you back, if I may, to the blue bag. When you saw that bag at your home, you immediately thought that it belonged to Mr. Agnes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. He brought it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you would have assumed, would you not, that its contents belonged to him?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you tell me why you were so interested to read through this military book that you saw inside?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Just like that, out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Simply curiosity; is that all?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the other matter I wanted to ask you about: You were asked a number of questions yesterday afternoon as to why it was out of the blue that you went to see Mirsad's mother at Tuzla. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you told Ms. Paterson that you had been thinking about Mirsad all this time, it wasn't just out of the blue. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What your answer was, was this: "I was thinking about him all the time, but I didn't have occasion to go there and to find him." Do you remember giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What was the occasion that led you to go on this particular -- at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: A friend of mine was going with me. First I went with a friend from Sarajevo, who was looking for the address to inquire whether he was in Tuzla. I didn't know whether he was in Tuzla. Then the friend from Sarajevo checked that he was there, and then I went to look for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This was the first that you'd heard that his mother was at Tuzla, or that he was at Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: His mother has a sister in Samac, and then I heard from a neighbour that they may be there, and then we called this gentleman in Sarajevo for him to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Ms. Marosevic. Can we go back to 1992, please. Can you please remind us what age you were at the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Nineteen. Eighteen, nineteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your father, what did he do for a living?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: He was working in Mebos, a company manufacturing boilers, water heaters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was he a powerful man, your father?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Has he been out of work for a number of years now?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that through his health?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Has he ever been politically active?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what training had you had prior to the war starting?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Catering school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So what sort of job were you looking for in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Something to do with catering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the job in the municipality building seem to you a good opportunity?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want to be clear about this. Did your family stay willingly in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you have Croat friends still in Bosanski Samac who stayed after the war?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to events after the war started. I think we are all agreed that the war started on about April the 16th or 17th in Samac?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, yesterday Ms. Paterson suggested to you a number of things which she said arose from the evidence of Mirsad Sahanic. I am going to invite you to comment on what Mirsad Sahanic in fact said in his evidence. So that everyone can follow this, page 187 of the transcript, lines 9 to 15. It was suggested to you yesterday that you couldn't possibly have taken food to Mirsad Sahanic in the elementary school in May because he was detained in Brcko at that time. In fact, his evidence is that he was detained in the elementary school in May. Is it your evidence that you took food to him in the elementary school in May?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was suggested to you yesterday that having obtained Mirsad's phone number, you made many, many phone calls to him. In fact, his evidence, page 200, is that you made four or five phone calls to him. Do you think you may have made that many phone calls to Mirsad, four or five?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I said that I had called him several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I want you to see if you can put a number on it. I think you said yesterday, at some stage, "a couple." Do you think it may have been as many as four or five phone calls?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. After you got his phone number, how long was it before you made the first phone call?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Quite a long time went by. I don't know exactly how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, are we talking about a few weeks, or a month or so?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I really can't remember exactly, but quite some time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, it was suggested to you yesterday by Ms. Paterson that you began these phone calls in the summer of 1998. In fact, when asked when the phone calls were, page 207, Mirsad Sahanic said all the phone calls from you were this year, 1999. Might that be right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I can't be quite sure, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, this is a curious way of re-examination, if I may say so. I know that Ms. Paterson asked the witness to comment at times upon the evidence given by Mirsad; there was no objection to it. But she was cross-examining. You're meant to be asking non-leading questions. I cannot imagine anything more leading than the nature of the questions you are putting. There's been no objection to it, but if you want us to place some value upon her answers, may I suggest you simply ask her the questions without giving her the hint of what Mirsad has already said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm simply seeking to create -- to repair questions that were asked in a wholly misleading form yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But that's something that you can do in address; but it doesn't help me, anyway, to have evidence from the witness who is being prompted in the way in which you are prompting her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I shan't proceed any further on that particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just one or two other things, please. Did Agnes ever say to you that he was going to get in touch with Mirsad Sahanic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The identification pass: Do you know what name Agnes was using in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you first saw that identification pass, the army pass, what name did it have in it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The bag: It was in a cupboard. Did you see it every day?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you put the towels in, where did you put them?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: In the bag, and then the bag in the cupboard. I zipped it up and put it in the cupboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But whereabouts in the bag did you put the towels?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you put them on top of the other stuff that was already in there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: I had to take things and put them in order and fold them up, so I don't remember exactly whether I put the towels on top or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you next opened the bag, in September, did it appear to be in the same state as it was when you had packed it up?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It hasn't been suggested to you, but I'm going to invite you to comment: Did you put the army pass in the bag at any time after Mr. Agnes left your house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you put anything else in the bag after Mr. Agnes left your house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA MAROSEVIC, Resumed
utterances.text: No, except the towels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marosevic, that completes your testimony, and you are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I start my testimony, may I be heard with a request, or an appeal? Actually, at the last hearing, Mr. Zecevic asked the Trial Chamber for the testimony of Mr. Drago Vukovic, Mr. Neskovic, and my own testimony to be heard in closed session, and he gave the reasons. I know that such a ruling was made with reference to Mr. Drago Vukovic, but I learnt yesterday that it was rejected with regard to the testimony of Mr. Neskovic. In view of the fact that I am the lead counsel for Mr. Milan Simic and that, through my testimony, I will certainly have to mention things linked to the strategy of defence of Milan Simic and other relevant matters which may affect the indictment case, it is my view that I should draw attention to this fact, that in this case, too, the same principle should apply as in the contempt hearing for Mr. Vujin, which was also held in closed session for the same reason. So I just wish to offer this additional argument, hoping that I could appeal to you to reconsider this request and hold the hearing in closed session during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, I listened to you and I heard you, but in actual fact, representations of that kind should really be made by your counsel, Mr. Haynes. We'll consider it. Mr. Ryneveld, what is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Our position is exactly the same today as it was yesterday. I might only say that the issue having been brought before the Chamber yesterday, and my request that you deal with the matter when issues arose, it's interesting to note that despite the fact that they indicated there should be a blanket, no issues arose. I pass that titbit of information on for the Court's consideration, but our position remains identical to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will adhere to the ruling that it gave yesterday. If, in the course of testimony, there is an intimation that something might be disclosed which would warrant a closed session, a closed hearing, then the Chamber will hear representations to that effect from counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder, before I begin examining this witness, whether the Trial Chamber might give me some indication of when we might take the mid-afternoon adjournment, because it would assist me as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take it at about 4 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your full name is Branislav Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you are 45 years of age?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You are a married man?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You have two children?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you are an attorney at law in private practice?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you been in private practice since 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Prior to which you worked in the law since 1978?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you've been employed as a lawyer in the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you've worked for the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if by that you mean work within the Ministry dealing with affairs relating to prosecution and people committing offences within the Ministry; that is to say, the employees of the Ministry. Then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think you've been a lecturer in criminal law and procedure?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had assignments of that kind, too, within the scope of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Since 1992, have you worked in an office that contained three attorneys?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have they always been the same people involved in that office?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning of my own private practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we heard a little about this from Mr. Vukovic, but perhaps you can tell us: Is that a cooperative, as it were? Do you all operate the same practice, or does each of you have a separate law practice?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, we each have separate law practices, but we just use the premises, the physical premises in which we sit, and we each contribute to the costs. But we all have separate practices with our own clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have to ask you this: Have you ever been charged or convicted of any criminal offence in your life?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in March of 1998, did you first become involved in the Bosanski Samac case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At whose invitation was that, and in what capacity were you first involved?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: At the request of Mr. Drago Vukovic, and I acted as his legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you assigned to be lead counsel to Mr. Milan Simic on the 7th of October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you were employed as a legal assistant -- that is, between March and October of 1998 -- can you tell us briefly what sort of work you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: In the first period, I worked -- I studied and read about the subject matter and problems in relation to the Tribunal, the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal, because this was my first case, and it demanded that I get to know the Rules of Procedure better. In the second phase -- that is to say from May, or somewhat later on -- I took a more direct involvement in preparing the defence case for Mr. Milan Simic, in the sense of helping Mr. Drago Vukovic with regard to some concrete tasks in the investigating process and in the collection of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may be obvious, but who was in charge at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the lead counsel was Mr. Drago Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you do things on your own initiative, or under his direction?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, never on my own initiative; always under his directions, the directions and guidelines given me by Mr. Drago Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we know that Mr. Vukovic resigned as lead counsel for Milan Simic; do you recall when you first learned that he might do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was perhaps the second half of August or the first half of September, but at any rate, when the indictment against Mr. Milan Simic was expanded to include persecution, and when it was obvious that the work of the Defence Counsel was becoming more complex, with the numerous new activities which emanated from this and would do so in the period to come. So that is how I came to see his line of reasoning. But from the beginning of September, he, himself, decided to step down and to leave the defence to me as counsel. Of course, Mr. Milan Simic made the final decision on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first hear of the witness Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: I first heard of Witness Agnes for the first time at the end of September -- or that is to say the end of August; I'm sorry, or the beginning of September, in one of the conversations that I had with my colleague, Mr. Vukovic, because we would frequently discuss the subject matter, the problems involved. But I didn't have occasion to see the witness or get to know him, because he had contacts with the witness. In fact, Drago Vukovic conveyed to me the fact that he had had a contact with -- contacts with two or three individuals who, in the meantime, contacted Mr. Vukovic. And Mr. Vukovic conveyed to me briefly information that he received from those individuals with whom he had had talks. And for two or three weekends I was out of Belgrade, and, as far as I was able to understand, he had these contacts with these individuals in precisely that period. One of those individuals was Mr. Agnes. And I remember that very well because he happened to mention some of his observations in that regard, and told me certain facts which were, for me, rather interesting. For example, he mentioned the fact that it was an individual who had a dual identity, who had two names; an individual who, according to what he said, had been in the army of the Republika Srpska; and that that particular gentleman, Mr. Agnes, had some problems. He was in prison, in fact, concerning some killing that occurred in a detention. So that I remember all these things, and he told me those facts in relation to that particular individual. Whereas he himself, Mr. Vukovic, was particularly interested; that is to say, he knew that I knew questions related to the state of citizens. And I remember that he asked me on the occasion whether it is possible for a refugee from the Republika Srpska to have -- go by another name; whether, according to our rules and regulations, this was at all possible. And I told him that this was absolutely impossible, in conformity with the laws of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which were in force at the time, and that this was a fact which was quite certainly, if it was done, was not done in conformity with the rules and regulations. Mr. Vukovic also drew my attention to other details linked to this particular individual, and those details referred to what he learnt from him. He told me that he had had a short conversation with him and that this came about via Ms. Jasna Marosevic. He told me that, for the most part, his testimony referred to the events in the primary school, and his claims that he had never seen Mr. Milan Simic. And basically he gave me a relatively negative picture of that particular individual, his discussion with him, and any possible future activities in this regard with respect to the defence of Mr. Milan Simic and our work on the Defence team. In September, mid-September, when Mr. Drago Vukovic decided to step down, he passed on all the documents concerning the case to me, because this was the stage in which I took up my role as lead counsel in the case. And so with Mr. Vukovic, as I say, I took all the documents he had to give me and took over the contacts that I did not have. And, amongst others, I remember that I talked about contacts with Mr. Agnes. But he told me at the time that he did not have -- he was not in touch with him because he had not left him any forwarding address, but that he would probably be contacting him, phoning him, and that he would probably be in touch in some way, if I was interested in getting to know him ultimately. The reason, apart from a formal one of getting in touch with him, regardless of the knowledge that Mr. Vukovic had, was that I should talk to this individual because, in the meantime, he could give me information on a persecution that was a topical subject, and one that hadn't been discussed by him with Mr. Vukovic, and to give me additional information linked to an identification of certain individuals who had been detained in the primary school building and who could be possible witnesses. According to Mr. Vukovic's assessment, that Mr. Agnes did know and could let us get into contact with certain individuals. I had lists of individuals of this kind, and this was a good occasion to have a conversation with him about all of that. So in that sense our contact did come about. Mr. Agnes phoned Mr. Vukovic, and Mr. Vukovic agreed upon a meeting, because we had already discussed this matter previously. This all took place in the space of several days, and it was relatively near Belgrade. It was a good opportunity for me to get to meet that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the first occasion that you met Mr. Agnes, how it was arranged, where it took place, and what transpired on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting took place in the town of Sremska Mitrovica on the 22nd of September, 1998, in the afternoon hours, just like according to the arrangement made by Mr. Vukovic after he had established contact and after having introduced me as the new counsel for Mr. Simic. We had agreed to meet in town across -- opposite the court in a sports hall, where there is several coffee bars. This was easy for both of us to find, and for us, because we had been to the courts. And at about 2 or 3 p.m. we arrived there, as agreed. I remember that we had to wait for quite a while for Mr. Agnes to turn up. I didn't know where he lived, nor did Drago Vukovic have any information as to his whereabouts, either his address or any other possibility of getting in touch with him, apart from waiting there, as we had agreed to do. So we waited for him for almost an hour, after which he turned up with a relative of his, and I got to know this on the occasion, and a boy, a 10 or 12 year old boy, I don't know who he was, but I thought at the time that it might be the son of the relation. So we sat down in the coffee bar. The coffee bar's name is Bingo and it is opposite the law courts. We had a brief conversation, discussing general subjects not related to the case. It was a general sort of talk, getting to know one another. And then Mr. Vukovic and myself got up with Mr. Agnes and we went for a walk, a stroll in the park nearby, so that we could discuss some matters linked to the case; that is to say the kind of conversation that Mr. Drago Vukovic had already had with him. Because we didn't want to discuss these matters in front of his relation and the little boy that we had met for the first time that day. And that's what we did. We spent -- we walked around for some half an hour, or 45 minutes. Drago Vukovic introduced me to Mr. Agnes. He said who I was. He said that I was on the Defence team for Mr. Milan Simic, that I had already been on the team for some time, and that I wanted to have some talks with him, and that I would like to keep in touch with him. And he agreed to this. He said there was no problems and that he didn't mind. He gave me some of the information that he gave to Mr. Drago Vukovic as well, relating to his general observations and the circumstances in 1992, and his whereabouts and movements in 1992; that he was detained at one point, and that during his detention in Brkco, Bijeljina, and then in the primary school building, and that he had joined up in the army of the Republika Srpska. But all this was very brief, because it was not an occasion to have an in-depth conversation about all of these things. So at the end of that meeting we decided to meet up again. This was perhaps Monday or Tuesday, and we decided on a meeting the following Monday, the following week. And he said that that was all right. Because I said that I would like to talk to him about certain things that Mr. Drago Vukovic hadn't discussed with him, and if he had more information to give me. He said that there was no problem and that we could go -- that we could have this meeting at the house of his relative. He gave me the address and told me how to find the house. And I found out that it was a house in the village of Martinci, which is about five or six kilometres away from the town of Sremska Mitrovica itself. We parted, and myself and Drago Vukovic returned to Belgrade, whereas Mr. Agnes, with his relation and that boy, went their way. And that was the meeting that we held on the 22nd of September in the town of Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am going to move on now to the next meeting. I am wondering if this is a good moment. This is a significant part of the case. I am perfectly happy to move on to it now, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Avramovic, you've told us about the meeting that took place on the 22nd of September in Sremska Mitrovica. Was that a meeting in which you took any note of what Mr. Agnes had to say?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the meeting on the 22nd, I did not take any particular notes on the spot, contemporaneously, but I took down the address that he gave me, because it was not technically possible to take notes, because most of the conversation took place while we were walking around and sitting on a bench very briefly in the park, so the whole conversation lasted perhaps a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Giving you his address, did you exchange any other contact details?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, except for the address and some general very brief information about the case itself, or rather his knowledge linked to events in 1992, there was no other discussion. The discussion centred on the matter that I was taking over the defence of Milan Simic and that I would like to have a lengthier discussion with him on the subject of the events of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Drago Vukovic have anything to do with the case after that date?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: After the 22nd, Drago Vukovic in effect no longer worked on the case, in terms of any contacts or activities in the field. As far as I can recollect that transitional period from the 22nd of September until my formal appointment as Defence counsel for Milan Simic, I can't really recollect the details, but I think that Drago Vukovic already then was withdrawing completely from the case, and he was focussing his attention on the office. If he dealt with the case at all, it was in his office, until he actually formally withdrew on the 7th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, so far as the next meeting was concerned, did you set a date on the 22nd of September for when that was going to be?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that we had fixed that date at the meeting on the 22nd. Why? Because that was a Monday, and this may have been a Tuesday or a Wednesday, so we said could we meet again next Monday; and Mr. Agnes said there would be no problems, that that suited him, that he would be at the home of his relatives, and he gave me the address and explained how I could get there and reach his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So did you go to his house on the 28th of September?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reserved that date for that conversation in my mind, and on Monday, without any announcement, as this had been arranged previously, I decided to travel to the village where he was living with his relatives. I remember that day very well, because Mr. Neskovic was in the office, and it was very lively because of his impending engagement as Defence counsel for Mr. Todorovic, and linked to his journey, which, as far as I can remember, was to take place the very next day. Bearing in mind the fact that Mr. Neskovic was formally the investigator in the Defence team for Milan Simic, and on the other hand, not wishing to travel alone to Martinci, I suggested to Mr. Neskovic that we go together. He was opposed, because he was preparing to leave, and he needed to do some additional things in connection with his visa, and he wasn't very keen regarding my suggestion that he come with me. However, just before I was about to leave, I saw him in the corridor and asked him once again to come with me, and he agreed, but on condition that we come back as quickly as possible. I told him that I didn't intend to stay for long, and that I, too, wanted to come home before dark -- before evening, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you find Mr. Agnes's address easily?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. The problem was mainly that even though there are streets with names in the village, the people in the village don't know the names of their own streets, so it was quite difficult to find that street, and we lost quite a bit of time to get to the address. Finally we arrived there, we entered the yard, and as far as I remember, I saw Mr. Agnes in the yard, in fact. I parked the car. He met us. I introduced Mr. Neskovic to him, because he didn't know him, and he led us into the house, which was 20 to 30 metres from the yard. We sat on the terrace of the house, and his relative was there, whom I had already met on the 22nd of September in Sremska Mitrovica. We sat at a table and started an informal conversation. I remember that well, because the conversation started in connection with the arrest of Mr. Stevan Todorovic, because the press had reported on it on that day, as well as the other media, so that everyone was aware of this event, and Mr. Neskovic said that he would be travelling to The Hague in that connection. This was an interesting subject because of the way in which the arrest had taken place, and the place, it being Serbia, and there were some comments exchanged on that topic. Then we went on to another topic, and I did not take part in that discussion. Mr. Neskovic and Mr. Agnes's relative started talking about some common acquaintances that they had from Bosnia, as his relative, as I learnt from the conversation, had lived for a time in Bosnia. As it was clear that we were wasting time, I suggested to Mr. Agnes that we go into a room where we could talk alone, and he said that there was no problem, he agreed, and we went into the dining room, where there was a big table. And, as I said a moment ago, I took with me the documentation, because I wanted to discuss some facts which Drago Vukovic had not discussed with Mr. Agnes, and to elucidate those facts if Mr. Agnes had had any knowledge about them. So I placed these documents on the table, and we started the conversation. Regarding the conversation itself, regarding the events in the elementary school, I can say that he was very brief.
